lead: Flexible drives carry power between shafts that sit far apart, using a member that bends — a belt, a chain or a wire rope — instead of gears that must mesh. After this unit you can pick the right drive for a duty, size a flat or V-belt for a given power and speed, select a roller chain, and choose a wire rope diameter and lay for a hoist.
about: The unit moves from the general to the specific. Chapter 6.1 sorts flexible drives into belts, chains and ropes and shows how a belt is built from cords and rubber, so the later chapters can talk about strength and friction. Chapter 6.2 designs a flat belt: centrifugal tension, the friction tension ratio and the belt width. Chapter 6.3 repeats this for a V-belt, using wedge-boosted friction and the belt-count procedure. Chapter 6.4 turns to chains, which remove slip but bring polygonal action, wear and a lubrication routine. Chapter 6.5 closes with wire ropes: construction, lays, bending over a sheave and selection from breaking strength. Every chapter reuses the stress, factor-of-safety and material tools from earlier units.

chapters.idea: A flexible drive transmits power through a member that bends around the pulleys or sprockets, so the shafts can be far apart and slightly misaligned; belts, chains and ropes differ only in how they grip and how much slip they allow.
chapters.depth: Classify the drives: flat belt, V-belt, round belt, timing (toothed) belt, chain, wire rope and fibre rope. Compare them with gears on centre distance, slip, shock absorption, cost and exactness of velocity ratio. Belt materials: leather (oak-tanned), cotton canvas, rubberised fabric, balata, and synthetics such as nylon, polyester and aramid cords. Belt construction: fabric plies, tension-carrying cords near the neutral axis, compression rubber below, covers on both faces; flat-belt joints (cemented, laced, hinged). V-belt sections A to E, groove angle 34° to 40°. Some syllabi call this topic flexible machine elements. Property values used later: leather density about 1000 kg/m³, coefficient of friction 0.25 to 0.4 for leather on cast iron.

figure.aria: A three-branch tree of flexible drives: belt splits into flat, V, round and timing belt; chain into roller and silent chain; rope into wire and fibre rope.

chapters.example: A leather belt is 100 mm wide and 6 mm thick and runs at 15 m/s. Leather density is 1000 kg/m³. Find the mass per metre length and the centrifugal tension. Mass per metre m = ρ b t = 1000 × 0.1 × 0.006 = 0.6 kg/m. Centrifugal tension Tc = m v² = 0.6 × 15² = 135 N. This 135 N pulls on the belt whether or not it carries load, so it is subtracted before the friction ratio is applied in 6.2.
chapters.trap: Assuming a V-belt grips on its flat bottom face. It grips on the two sloping sides; the bottom must clear the groove bottom, otherwise the wedge action is lost and the drive behaves like a poor flat belt.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, for material properties, density and the idea of a design factor.
chapters.leave: Stress design of flat and V-belts to 6.2 and 6.3; chain and rope detail to 6.4 and 6.5; pulley and shaft sizing to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A flat belt drives by friction over part of the pulley rim, so the tight-side and slack-side tensions are tied by the ratio e to the power μθ, and design means choosing a belt width large enough that the required tensions never exceed the belt's strength.
chapters.depth: Velocity ratio N₁d₁ = N₂d₂ with slip allowed for. Arc of contact on the smaller pulley: open belt θd = 180° − 2 sin⁻¹((D − d)/2C); crossed belt θd = 180° + 2 sin⁻¹((D + d)/2C). Belt length for open and crossed drives. Centrifugal tension Tc = m v², with m = ρ b t. Maximum tension T = σ b t, where σ is the safe stress, b the width and t the thickness. Friction condition (T₁ − Tc)/(T₂ − Tc) = e^(μθ), with θ in radians. Power = (T₁ − T₂)v. Initial tension T₀ = (T₁ + T₂)/2 + Tc. Maximum power occurs at Tc = T/3, that is v = √(T/3m); for T = 1000 N and m = 0.6 kg/m this gives 23.6 m/s. Creep, slip and the design steps in order.

figure.aria: A curve of transmitted power against belt speed that rises to a peak near 24 m/s and then falls, marking the maximum power point.

chapters.example: A 15 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a line shaft at 480 rpm through an open flat belt. Pulley diameters 200 mm and 600 mm, centre distance 2 m, μ = 0.3, belt thickness 10 mm, density 1000 kg/m³, safe stress 2.5 N/mm². Find the belt width. v = π × 0.2 × 1440/60 = 15.08 m/s. θd = 180 − 2 sin⁻¹(400/4000) = 168.5° = 2.94 rad; μθ = 0.882, e^0.882 = 2.416. T₁ − T₂ = 15000/15.08 = 994.7 N, so T₂ = 702.5 N and T₁ = 1697.2 N. With b in mm, Tc = 2.274b N and T = 25b N. Then 1697.2 + 2.274b = 25b gives b = 74.7 mm; take 80 mm.
chapters.trap: Using 180° as the arc of contact, or feeding degrees into e^(μθ). Use the smaller pulley's arc, converted to radians.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for belt materials, thickness and density; Unit 1 for direct stress and factor of safety.
chapters.leave: V-belt wedge friction and belt counting to 6.3; shaft and bearing reactions from the belt pull to Unit 3 and Unit 5; belt fatigue to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A V-belt sits in a groove and wedges into it, so the effective friction is μ/sin β instead of μ — around three times larger — which lets a V-drive work on short centre distances with small pulleys, at the cost of rating the drive as a number of standard belts.
chapters.depth: Standard sections A to E: A is 13 mm wide and 8 mm thick, B is 17 mm and 11 mm, and larger sections follow; belt designation such as B 1000 means section B, pitch length 1000 mm. Groove angle 2β = 34° to 40°, narrowing on small pulleys as the belt bends. Effective friction μ′ = μ/sin β, tension ratio (T₁ − Tc)/(T₂ − Tc) = e^(μθ/sin β). Rated power per belt from a rating chart at the given speed and pitch diameter. Correction factors: arc of contact factor and belt length factor. Number of belts = design power ÷ (rated power × arc factor × length factor), rounded up; keep it under about eight. Service factor from duty and running hours. Belt speed limit about 25 m/s. V-flat drives. Tensioning and take-up.

figure.aria: A six-step flowchart from design power to the number of V-belts, passing through section choice, pulley diameters, rated power and correction factors.

chapters.example: A 7.5 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a compressor at 480 rpm for two shifts, so the service factor is 1.2. Design power = 7.5 × 1.2 = 9 kW. Use a B-section belt with pitch diameters 140 mm and 420 mm and centre distance 420 mm. Belt speed v = π × 0.14 × 1440/60 = 10.56 m/s. The rating chart gives 2.6 kW per belt. Arc: (420 − 140)/420 = 0.667, sin⁻¹(0.333) = 19.47°, θd = 141°, arc factor 0.87. Length factor 0.95. Number of belts = 9 ÷ (2.6 × 0.87 × 0.95) = 9 ÷ 2.149 = 4.19, so use 5 belts.
chapters.trap: Treating the groove angle as β when the formula needs the half angle. If 2β = 38°, then sin β = sin 19°, and μ′ ≈ 3.1μ. Using sin 38° gives roughly half that and a badly oversized drive.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for the tension ratio, centrifugal tension and power relation; 6.1 for belt construction and friction values.
chapters.leave: Chain drives to 6.4; groove cutting and pulley materials are outside this unit; bearing loads from the two belt pulls to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A chain pulls through rollers seated in sprocket teeth, so it gives an exact velocity ratio with no slip, but each link moves as a chord of a polygon, which adds speed fluctuation, wear and a lubrication requirement.
chapters.depth: Types: bush roller and roller chain, silent (inverted tooth) chain, block chain, detachable chain. Parts of a roller chain: pin, bush, roller, inner and outer plates; ISO designation 08B, 10B and ANSI 40, 50 as the standard way to specify. Pitch p, roller diameter, inner width. Pitch line velocity v = Z p N/60; pitch diameter d = p/sin(180/Z). Chordal (polygonal) action: speed varies by the factor cos(180/Z), so keep at least 17 teeth on the small sprocket, 19 or more for smooth running. Chain length in pitches L = 2C/p + (Z₁ + Z₂)/2 + ((Z₂ − Z₁)/2π)² p/C, rounded to an even number of links. Failures: fatigue of plates, wear of pins, bushes and rollers, galling, elongation and jumping the tooth, roller breakage. Selection: service factor × power = design power, pick sprocket teeth and chain number from the rating chart, fix centre distance. Lubrication: brush, drip, bath, disc, spray; sag and adjustment.

figure.aria: A falling curve of percentage chain speed variation against the number of teeth on the small sprocket, about 4 percent at 11 teeth and 1.4 percent at 19 teeth.

chapters.example: A 7.5 kW motor at 1000 rpm drives a compressor through a single-strand 08B roller chain of pitch 12.7 mm, with Z₁ = 19 and Z₂ = 38 teeth and a centre distance of 500 mm. Find the chain speed, the chain length and the factor of safety if the catalogue gives a breaking load of 18 kN. Pitch diameter d₁ = p/sin(180/Z₁) = 12.7/sin 9.474° = 77.16 mm. v = π × 0.07716 × 1000/60 = 4.04 m/s. Tension = 7500/4.04 = 1856 N, so factor of safety = 18000/1856 = 9.7. Length L = 78.74 + 28.5 + 0.23 = 107.5, so use 108 links. Speed variation = 1 − cos(180/19) = 1.36%.
chapters.trap: Rounding the chain length to an odd number of links. An odd count needs an offset link, which is weaker than a normal link; always round up to an even number and shorten the centre distance instead.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for where a chain sits among flexible drives; 6.3 for the service-factor habit of mind.
chapters.leave: Sprocket tooth profile and manufacturing; gears and gearboxes for exact ratios under heavy load to Unit 7; shaft and bearing loads to Unit 3 and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A wire rope carries load only in tension, and its strength comes from many small wires sharing the pull, so selection means choosing construction and lay, sizing the diameter from the breaking strength with a factor of safety, and keeping the sheave large enough to hold bending stress down.
chapters.depth: Constructions 6×7, 6×19, 6×37, 6×61 and 8×19: the first number is strands, the second is wires per strand. Fibre core (sisal, manila, hemp) against steel core, written IWRC. Spiral strand and locked coil ropes for standing duty. Lays: regular (cross) lay and lang lay, each right-hand or left-hand; lay length; lang lay is more flexible and wears longer but tends to untwist under load, regular lay is stable and the usual default. Stresses: direct σt = W/A with A = k(π/4)d², fill factor k about 0.4 for 6×19; bending σb = E_w δ/D, where E_w = 2×10⁵ N/mm² is the wire modulus, δ the wire diameter (about d/15 for 6×19) and D the sheave or drum diameter. Keep D/d at 30 or more, higher for fast hoists. Selection: factor of safety about 5 to 8 by duty, breaking strength = factor × load, read off the diameter, then check D/d. Rope efficiency in multi-fall systems.

figure.aria: The layers of a 6×19 rope from the outer wires of a strand inward to the core, drawn as nested layers.

chapters.example: A lift cage and its load weigh 1000 kg and hang on a 6×19 wire rope with a fibre core, of ultimate strength 1400 N/mm², over a sheave of 500 mm. Use a factor of safety of 6. Find the rope diameter and the bending stress. Load W = 1000 × 9.81 = 9810 N; breaking load needed = 6 × 9810 = 58 860 N. With A = 0.4d², breaking load = 1400 × 0.4d² = 560d² N, so d² = 105.1 and d = 10.25 mm; take 11 mm. Check D/d = 500/11 = 45, above the 40 wanted for a lift. Wire diameter δ ≈ 11/15 = 0.733 mm, so σb = 2×10⁵ × 0.733/500 = 293 N/mm², against direct stress σt = 9810/(0.4 × 121) = 203 N/mm².
chapters.trap: Applying the factor of safety to the sum of direct and bending stress. The factor of safety is applied to the tensile breaking load of the whole rope; bending is controlled by keeping D/d large, not by adding stresses and dividing.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the place of rope among flexible drives; Unit 1 for direct stress and factor of safety.
chapters.leave: Drum, sheave and brake design to Unit 3; wire fatigue under repeated bending beyond the D/d rule; chain and belt comparisons back to 6.4 and 6.2.

links: belt material and thickness set the safe stress σ in the flat belt design
the friction ratio e^(μθ) becomes e^(μθ/sin β) once the belt wedges into a groove
chains are chosen when the slip of a belt cannot be accepted
tension ratio, centrifugal effect and factor of safety carry straight over to ropes
both are table-selected metal elements sized by load, speed and a service factor
